title: Trajectory fit alone does not identify causal edges: a white-box masked ODE benchmark for trans-omics digital twins of drug action mechanisms
authors: Zhang, Z.; Jia, L.; Pan, Y.; Zhao, H.
abstract: Dynamic multi-omics models infer drug mechanisms from trajectories, but trajectory accuracy alone cannot verify that learned regulatory edges are mechanistically correct. We asked to what extent fitting time-series dynamics identifies intervenable causal edges across observation and optimization budgets.We built white-box ordinary differential equations with candidate-edge masks for gene-expression, protein, signalling and metabolite dynamics, using a mouse-liver trans-omics topology and ground-truth semi-synthetic time series. Under noise-free,complete, densely sampled data, from-scratch training ranked edges near chance(edge-class area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve, 0.48-0.53); the unattainable oracle-initialized upper bound reached 0.94-0.99 on the same metric.Unobserved layers absorbed error. In ground-truth knockout tests, development-batch endpoint-sign accuracy was 67.9% for one-hop non-convergent targets but 33.3% for two-hop targets. Across tested practical budgets, fitting did not yield reliable edge recovery; trajectory fit alone therefore does not establish mechanistic identification. This benchmark supports mechanistic audits and exploratory per-prediction confidence grading in multi-omics models.

title: Comparative Mitogenomics and Molecular Phylogeny of Agriculturally Significant Tephritid Fruit Fly Pests in Bangladesh
abstract: Tephritid fruit flies of the tribe Dacini rank among the most economically destructive agricultural pests globally, with several species of Bactrocera Macquart and Zeugodacus Hendel causing severe losses to fruit and vegetable production across South and Southeast Asia. Bangladesh harbors several economically important dacine species, including Bactrocera dorsalis (Hendel), B. carambolae (Drew & Hancock), B. zonata (Saunders), B. correcta (Bezzi) and Zeugodacus cucurbitae (Coquillett). Here we present a comparative mitogenomic and phylogenetic framework based on 21 unique GenBank mitogenome records: 19 dacine ingroup records and two outgroups. The ingroup includes B. papayae, B. philippinensis and B. invadens, whose synonymy with B. dorsalis is disputed. All records contained 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs) and two rRNA genes. Genome size in the 14 taxa of subgenus Bactrocera ranged from 15,273 to 15,977 bp. Whole-genome AT content ranged from 66.6% in B. tsuneonis to 82.2% in Drosophila melanogaster, and the five focal pest species clustered at 72.9-73.6%. Maximum-likelihood analysis of a 13,600-site alignment (13 PCGs plus 12S and 16S rRNA; GTR+FO; IQ-TREE v1.6.11; 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, UFBoot) recovered the B. dorsalis complex (UFBoot = 100), within which pairwise distances were only 0.64-1.33%, and a B. correcta + B. zonata pair (UFBoot = 100). Nine taxa showed compositional heterogeneity and third codon positions were highly variable, so deeper nodes should be interpreted cautiously. As no Bangladeshi specimens were sequenced, this study is a curated reference baseline for molecular identification and pest surveillance, not a population-genomic analysis.

title: Identification of SAMD4B as a Centrosome-Associated Regulator of the Sonic Hedgehog Signaling Pathway
authors: Bernatik, O.; Vyslouzil, D.; Paclikova, P.; Renzova, T.; Kovarikova, P.; Cajanek, L.
abstract: Background: Many protein-protein interactions are required for the assembly and function of primary cilia, microtubule-based organelles critical for the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway and, in turn, for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis. However, our understanding of this complex process remains incomplete. Methods: To identify new regulators of primary cilia formation or function, we carried out proximity labeling experiments and compared interactomes under ciliogenesis-restrictive and permissive conditions. Using an unbiased strategy, we selected candidates that were tested functionally by siRNA-mediated depletion or gene editing, in combination with gene expression analysis and various microscopy techniques, using either vertebrate cell lines or zebrafish as model systems. Results: We demonstrate that one of our identified candidates, protein SAMD4B, is associated with the centrosome and is required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish. Our data implicate defective ciliary recruitment of Shh pathway regulators ARL13B and SMO as a plausible mechanism underlying the SAMD4B-mediated regulation of Shh signaling. Conclusions: Together, our data identify a previously unrecognized link between SAMD4B, a protein known to be associated with cytoplasmic RNA condensates, and ciliary signaling.

title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
authors: Bunterngchit, C.; Aslam, S.; Sattar, A.; Rasool, A.; Wang, Y.
abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
authors: Yamauchi, R.; Tsukiyama, S.; Sato, K.
abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
authors: Uddin, M. M.; Khan, S. M. Z. A.; Bomma Yadagiri, K.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

title: Beta-cell-derived urocortin-3 contributes to glucose-regulated somatostatin and glucagon secretion in the mouse pancreas
authors: Vergara-Ucin, J.; Andersen, D. B.; di Giuseppe, G.; Mezza, T.; Rosenkilde, M.; Holst, J. J.
abstract: Aims/Hypothesis. Glucagon secretion is impaired in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The mechanisms behind this dysregulation are incompletely understood. Urocortin-3 (UCN-3), a beta-cell-derived peptide, stimulates somatostatin (SST) secretion and may thereby regulate glucagon secretion. We investigated the mechanisms through which UCN-3 regulates pancreatic hormone secretion and examined the physiological contribution of endogenous UCN-3 to glucose-regulated hormone secretion. Methods. Pancreatic hormone secretion was studied using the isolated perfused mouse pancreas. The effects of exogenous and endogenous UCN-3 were investigated using selective antagonists of SST receptors (SSTR) and corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 2 (CRHR2). In addition, the role of UCN-3 was examined in streptozotocin (STZ) treated mice. Results. Exogenous UCN-3stimulated somatostatin secretion and inhibited glucagon secretion in the mouse pancreas. Blockade of SSTRs completely abolished the glucagonostatic effect of UCN-3, demonstrating that inhibition of glucagon secretion is indirectly mediated through SST signaling. Moreover, CRHR2 antagonism prevented both UCN-3-induced SST secretion and inhibition of glucagon secretion, identifying CRHR2 as the key receptor mediating these effects. During acute glucose stimulation (3.5-10mM), CRHR2 antagonism reduced glucose-induced stimulation of SST and attenuated glucagon inhibition, indicating that endogenous UCN-3 participates in the acute islet response to hyperglycemia. However, during sustained hyperglycemia, CRHR2 antagonism reduced SST secretion without altering glucagon secretion. In STZ-treated mice, glucose-induced SST secretion was lost. Conclusions. Urocortin-3 regulated glucagon secretion indirectly through CRHR2-dependent stimulation of SST secretion. Endogenous UCN-3 contributes to the acute islet response to hyperglycemia, supporting a physiologically relevant beta-cell-to-delta-cell-to-alpha-cell paracrine axis in the mouse pancreas. This pathway is disrupted following beta-cell loss, suggesting a potential contribution to impaired islet hormone regulation in diabetes.

title: Palmitic acid overload does not promote full-blown dysfunction in SGBS adipocytes which is reflected in their secretome
authors: Angelini, S.; Stifani, G.; La Runa, G.; Cosenza, L. C.; Lodi, G.; Voltan, R.; Secchiero, P.; Castaldo, F.; Gessi, S.; Merighi, S.; Fernandez, M.; Bigot, A.; Wabitsch, M.; Cervellati, C.; Sanz, J. M.; Passaro, A.; Sergi, D.
abstract: Background: Energy excess, and particularly long-chain saturated fatty acid (SFA) overload, are instrumental in promoting obesity and hampering metabolic health. However, SFA contribution to human adipocyte metabolic and endocrine dysfunction remains elusive. Nonetheless, we have already provided evidence that a 48-hour palmitic acid (PA) exposure is not sufficient to hamper Simpson-Golabi Behmel Syndrome (SGBS) adipocytes insulin signalling. Objective: This study aims at evaluating whether a 96-hour exposure to PA is able to disrupt SGBS adipocyte metabolic health and induce the release of a secretome capable of hampering insulin signalling in skeletal muscle cells. Methods: SGBS adipocytes were treated with either 1000 uM PA or bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 96 hours followed by the assessment of the NFkB signalling and the expression of genes associate with inflammation and adipocyte metabolic stress. Furthermore, adipocytes were labelled with BODIPY and lipid droplet as well as cell size semi-quantified using ImageJ. Insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt and Akt substrate of 160 kDa (AS160) was assessed by Western Blot. The effect of PA on SGBS secretome was assessed by both ELISA as well as MILLIPLEX. Finally, human immortalised myotubes were co-cultured with BSA or PA-treated SGBS adipocytes for 24 hours followed by the assessment of insulin signalling at the Akt level. Results: PA did not activate the NFkB signalling pathway, but induced the expression of MCP-1 while tending to upregulate IL-6 mRNA levels. Despite 96-hour PA exposure leading to an increase in lipid droplet and cell size, this was not coupled with an impairment in insulin signalling. Nevertheless, this SFA promoted an increase in IL-6 and IL-8 secretion while tending to enhance the release of adiponectin by SGBS adipocytes. Finally, the secretome from PA-treated SGBS adipocyte did not impair insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt relative to controls in myotubes. Conclusions: Thus, in the absence of the stromal vascular fraction, direct exposure of SGBS adipocytes to PA overload is not sufficient to elicit overt dysfunction. The absence of full-blown adipocyte dysfunction is reflected in the secretome of these cells which failed to disrupt skeletal muscle insulin signalling.

title: Comparative transcriptomics reveals shared and context-dependent adaptations of bovine cells across culture systems for cultivated meat
authors: Ribarski-Chorev, I.; Burghardt, M.; Tawil, S.; Gershkoviz, A.; Shpatz, D.; Schudy, G.; Beh Hamo, Y.; Gilad, Y.; Vainshtein, I.; Kfir, A.; Tuller, T.; Schlesinger, S.
abstract: Developing cell-culture systems for cultivated meat requires understanding how candidate cells respond to prolonged expansion and different growth environments. However, the extent to which bovine cells share transcriptional adaptations across these conditions, or retain responses specific to their origin and cellular state, remains unclear. Here, we systematically profiled bovine umbilical cord (BUC)- and adipose tissue (BAT)-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) across different culture architectures, passage stages, and differentiation states, including immortalized BUC cells and satellite cells as a myogenic reference. We show that global transcriptomic variation is strongly associated with culture architecture, cell identity, and cellular state. Immortalization preserved several early-passage transcriptional features, particularly proliferation-related programs, while opposing selected changes associated with primary cell aging. Culture architecture induced distinct rather than uniform three-dimensional responses. Spheroid formation produced a pronounced transcriptional shift characterized by reduced proliferation-, chromatin-, and development-associated programs, alongside changes in extracellular-matrix organization, metabolism, and intracellular remodeling. Across primary umbilical cord-derived, adipose-derived, and myogenically induced umbilical cord-derived cells, scaffold-versus-plate comparisons revealed correlated but non-identical transcriptional responses. These involved changes in extracellular-matrix organization, adhesion, membrane trafficking, and developmental pathways, with endocytosis enriched across all three comparisons among the pathways examined. During myogenic induction, both satellite cells and BUC-derived cells exhibited muscle-related cytoskeletal and contractile programs, while scaffold culture further supported myogenic signatures in BUC-derived cells. These findings distinguish recurring culture-associated responses from transcriptional features tied to cell source and expansion history. They support evaluating cultivated-meat candidate cells in their intended culture systems, not solely under conventional plate conditions.

title: Large-scale Nanopore sequencing resolves species diversity and distribution of European Ulva
authors: van der Loos, L. M.; D'hondt, S.; Coulembier Vandelannoote, E.; Bafort, Q.; Casteleyn, G.; Akdogan Sirin, P.; Accoroni, S.; Ahsan, U.; Albert, G.; Arenas, F.; Armeli Minicante, S.; Aruci, E.; Bakratsas, G.; Balina, K.; Barboza, F. R.; Barda, I.; Bartolo, A.; Bartsch, I.; Becker, J.; Belattmania, Z.; Bellanti, G.; Bermejo, R.; Bernardi Aubry, F.; Bizien, A.; Blanfune, A.; Blomme, J.; Bo Rasmussen, M.; Boderskov, T.; Bonacic, K.; Bourgougnon, N.; Brazier, P.; Brodie, J.; Bruhn, A.; Bunker, F.; Burel, T.; Camus, J.; Canning-Clode, J.; Chemodanov, A.; Courtois de Vicose, G.; Cremades, J.; Dake, A.
abstract: The green algal genus Ulva is widespread and ecologically important in European coastal ecosystems. However, species diversity and distributions remain poorly resolved due to phenotypic plasticity and historical taxonomic uncertainty. By adopting a large-scale sampling and barcoding effort, we provide a unique continent-scale assessment of Ulva species diversity and distribution. We developed a novel high-throughput Oxford Nanopore Technologies sequencing strategy, pooling 768 samples (eight 96-well plates) per run and sequencing tufA and ITS simultaneously. Nanopore barcoding was accurate and efficient, with 96.3% of samples yielding at least one informative marker. Consensus sequences showed 99.4-100% similarity to Sanger sequences. By analysing 3,657 samples from 30 countries, we identified 46 species with contrasting distribution patterns and substantially expanded their known geographic ranges. This includes numerous country-level first records and the first records of Ulva howensis outside Australia and U. meridionalis within the study area. Five non-indigenous Ulva species were also detected, including widespread occurrences of U. australis. However, 10 species could not be assigned to named taxa because suitable reference sequences were unavailable or unreliable, highlighting persistent taxonomic gaps in public databases. Our findings demonstrate the power of coordinated, high-throughput molecular surveys to resolve cryptic marine biogeography at continent scales. The resulting high-resolution spatial baseline facilitates the early detection of non-indigenous species and range expansions. It also enables coastal managers to monitor invasion pathways, evaluate ecosystem risks associated with opportunistic bloom-forming taxa, and detect climate-driven distribution shifts across European waters.

title: ChIP-seq analysis of SMAD3 target genes in a sea anemone reveals symbiosis-dependent regulation through TGF-β signaling
authors: Burleigh, O. L.; Dix, M. F.; Ruggeri, M.; Cui, G.; Aranda, M.; Weis, V. M.
abstract: Background: Cnidarian-algal symbiosis underpins coral reefs, but elevated temperatures can disrupt it, causing bleaching. Bleaching activates host stress and immune pathways and disrupts symbiotic signaling and nutrient transfer. Among these pathways, the immunosuppressive cytokine transforming growth factor-{beta} (TGF-{beta}) promotes host tolerance of symbionts in cnidarians, but the genes regulated by its transcription factor, SMAD3, remain unknown. SMAD3 ChIP-seq and RNA-seq were used to identify putative targets in symbiotic and aposymbiotic Exaiptasia diaphana after 6 and 18 h of heat stress. Results: SMAD3 binding was highly specific to each combination of symbiotic state and heat treatment. Symbiotic state, not heat stress, drove most differential binding, with binding nearly always higher in symbiotic animals. Integration identified 625 putative targets differentially bound and expressed between symbiotic states. Differential binding between symbiotic states peaked at 18 h, when these targets made up the largest share of symbiosis-associated expression differences. Activation targets suggest SMAD3 supports symbiosis through the mucociliary surface, host control of nitrogen available to symbionts, uptake of symbiont-derived retinoids, and immunity. Repression targets, which outnumbered activation targets at 18 h, suggest SMAD3 limits canonical sterol transport, alters G protein-coupled receptor expression, and may reinforce its own activity by repressing negative regulators of TGF-{beta} signaling. Conclusions: SMAD3 appears to act as a bifunctional regulator whose binding is shaped primarily by symbiotic state. Its putative targets suggest roles in cnidarian symbiosis beyond immune suppression, including nutrient exchange and retinoid signaling. These findings provide a framework for TGF-{beta} function in cnidarian symbiosis and thermal stress.

title: 2-hydroxyglutarate-dependent inhibition of TET2 is a molecular link between metabolic reprogramming and smooth muscle cell differentiation
authors: Kwartler, C. S.; Esparza Pinelo, J. E.; Robin, A. M.; Richard, A.; Dosunmu, A. O.; Garcia Serrano, J.; Gonzalez Hernandez, A. D.; Krenz, H.; Chen, J.; Carrera, M.; Bornes, K. E.; Roy, S. S.; Chatthopadhyay, A.; Milewicz, D. M.; Gottlieb, E.
abstract: Background: Smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypic modulation is accompanied by metabolic reprogramming, but the mechanisms linking metabolism to contractile gene expression remain unclear. We investigated whether 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), an inhibitor of ?-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, links metabolic changes to regulation of ten-eleven translocation 2 (TET2) in Acta2R179C/+ SMCs Methods: Primary wild-type (WT) and Acta2R179C/+ mouse aortic SMCs were treated with nicotinamide riboside (NR), exogenous R&L-2-HG, or cholesterol. Endogenous accumulation of L-2HG was achieved by lentivuris-mediated knockdown (KD) of L2hgdh. We assessed contractile marker expression, cellular metabolism, TET2 chromatin occupancy, and DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation. L-2HG levels were assessed using liquid chromatography/mass spectroscopy. Carotid artery 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) staining was assessed in mice after left carotid artery ligation. Results: Acta2R179C/+ SMCs have elevated 2-HG, reduced TET2 expression and chromatin occupancy, and lower 5hmC enrichment at CArG-containing SMC loci, consistent with repressed TET2 activity. NR boosts oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), reduces 2-HG in WT and mutant SMCs, increases TET2 expression and 5hmC enrichment, and reduces global 5-methylcytosine. Carotid artery 5hmC staining shows changes in the same direction, but group differences are not statistically significant. Exogenous L-2-HG attenuates NR-induced contractile marker expression in Acta2R179C/+ SMCs and also decreases contractile marker expression, reduces TET2 occupancy and 5hmC enrichment, and shifts WT SMC metabolism toward glycolysis, phenocopying the metabolic state of Acta2R179C/+ SMCs. Endogenous accumulation of L-2HG by L2hgdh KD reduces contractile markers in WT SMCS. Cholesterol reduces TET2 and contractile marker expression, decreases 5hmC enrichment, and increases global DNA methylation. Conclusions: These findings support a role for 2-HG in coupling metabolic state to epigenetic changes associated with SMC phenotypic modulation. NR-associated differentiation coincides with increased TET2 expression and DNA hydroxymethylation, identifying metabolic regulation of the SMC epigenome as a potential approach to preserving contractile gene expression.

title: The genetic architecture of lipoprotein(a): simplicity, complexity, and mutability
authors: Mukamel, R. E.; Rubinacci, S.; Kamitaki, N.; Handsaker, R. E.; Hujoel, M. L. A.; Tang, D.; McCarroll, S. A.; Loh, P.-R.
abstract: High levels of lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) increase risk of cardiovascular diseases. Lp(a) concentration is primarily determined (>80%) by genetic variation at LPA, particularly by its large, size-polymorphic kringle IV-2 (KIV-2) repeat. However, because variation of the KIV-2 repeat is difficult to measure, the precise ways that genetic variants at LPA and other loci determine Lp(a) levels have been unclear, especially in individuals of non-European ancestry. Here, we developed new computational techniques to accurately genotype KIV-2 variation in whole-genome-sequenced population cohorts. Applying these methods to UK Biobank (n=490,414) and All of Us (n=245,394) provided insights into the genetic determinants of Lp(a) and the mutational dynamics of the KIV-2 repeat, which we found expands or contracts intra-allelically once every [~]500 generations. Variation in Lp(a) levels among people of all genetic ancestries was accurately predicted by a single, transferable genetic model capturing cis-epistatic effects of KIV-2 length and protein-altering polymorphisms in LPA. Controlling for predicted effects of LPA alleles revealed an additional, highly polygenic contribution to Lp(a) variation: LPA-adjusted Lp(a) levels associated with genetic variation at over 300 loci (P<5x10-8), much like other blood lipids. These results elucidate the genetic architecture and mutational origins of Lp(a) variation, showing how detailed characterization of a largely monogenic trait can provide surprising insights for complex trait genetics.

title: Improving Target-Adverse Event Association Prediction via Inverse Node Frequency Transformation to Mitigate Knowledge Graph Topological Bias
authors: Egbelo, T. M.; Jeynes, J. C. G.; Kurt, Z.; Veettil, R. V.; Gillet, V. J.
abstract: Motivation: Identifying significant associations between therapeutic protein targets and adverse events (AEs) is a critical component of drug safety assessment. To accelerate the process, machine learning methods have been developed to predict these associations as edges in network data integrating molecular interactions and other key biomedical knowledge. However, these networks often suffer from topological imbalances where a minority of "hub" nodes determine the predictive signal. This "topological" or "degree bias" can lead to poor performance on novel or understudied targets where safety inference is most needed. Results: We introduce Inverse Node Frequency (INF), a generally applicable node degree-based approach for mitigating topological bias. Employing an enriched biomedical knowledge graph and our own carefully curated target-adverse event associations, we apply INF as a normalisation procedure on a class of graph-derived features called metapaths and evaluate their resulting target-AE association prediction performance. Our results demonstrate that INF significantly improves the true positive rate (TPR/recall) for low-degree targets compared to the untransformed metapath features as well as a popular established normalisation method, while also achieving highly competitive hits@k, a ranking-based metric for knowledge graph-based inference. We also evaluated INF on an external set of target-AE associations never before used for modelling, on which INF also showed superior resilience compared to the two benchmarks.

title: Ionic waves drive fluid flow by inducing spatiotemporal porosity variations in the brain interstitial space
abstract: We develop a model of interstitial fluid (ISF) dynamics in the brain driven by traveling ionic waves. The cortex is modeled as a 2D porous sheet with an absorbent matrix. A prescribed 10% sinusoidal porosity variation induces mean flow of O(1) {micro}m/s, even without an imposed pressure gradient. Including perivascular spaces (PVSs) increases the velocity and pressure gradient, and yields volumetric flux through arterial and venous PVSs, with maximum magnitude of 2 x 10-2 {micro}L min-1 mm-1. We show analytically, in the large-wavelength limit, that the porosity variation enters the pressure field as first- and second-order corrections. We then simulate a physiologically realistic spreading depolarization (SD) wave, finding that the induced porosity variation raises the mean ISF pressure to 4 mmHg, which falls to -0.7 mmHg during recovery. SD yields a peak velocity of O(10-2) {micro}m/s and a peak flux of 3 x 10-3 {micro}L min-1 mm-1, and transiently stalls the PVS-driven flow. Although the SD wave produces a larger porosity change than the prescribed wave, it evolves slowly and drives weaker flow.

title: Koopman Analysis Reveals Collective Modes Governing Cellular Dynamics
authors: Dutta, S.; Yu, W.; Zheng, Z.; Giri, A.; Xing, J.
abstract: Living systems are complex nonlinear systems that operate far from thermodynamic equilibrium, and this nonlinearity makes their dynamics difficult to analyze. Several linearization techniques have been developed to address this problem, but most are local. Koopman operator theory is a powerful alternative that linearizes a system globally. Here we show that it not only achieves global linearization but also reveals collective modes that govern the dynamics of complex, out-of-equilibrium nonlinear systems. Applying the approach to whole-cell dynamical models, we find that these collective modes have physical and biological significance and relate to distinct processes in the cell cycle and in cell-state transitions. Collective and normal modes are widespread in many-body systems, particularly in condensed matter (e.g., magnons, phonons, hydrodynamic modes) and in macromolecular dynamics (e.g., normal mode analysis). By demonstrating that such modes also exist in cell-state transition dynamics, and in non-equilibrium nonlinear systems more generally, we offer a new theoretical-physics perspective on these systems. The collective modes separate into slow and fast modes. Long-term dynamics are governed by a few dominant slow modes that form a slow manifold of much lower dimension than the original state space. Thus, although the cell is a very high-dimensional system, its cell-cycle dynamics ultimately reduce to a low-dimensional space. Each mode comprises the coordinated behavior of groups of genes and reflects the structure of the underlying gene regulatory network. The modes can also be decomposed into terms that behave like damped harmonic oscillators, drawing an analogy between the modes of a nonlinear system and the normal modes of many-body systems. Finally, our analysis suggests that the dominant modes are closely associated with biological processes in the cell cycle, including mitosis, spindle checkpoint signaling, and DNA replication and repair.
